official_measurement_examples.name: Stopping up definition
official_measurement_examples.fact: Stopping up is the legal process that removes highway rights to permanently close or divert a highway; planning permission alone does not remove those rights.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 247
official_measurement_examples.fact: Section 247 is used to stop up or divert highways to enable approved development, subject to the statutory order process.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 253
official_measurement_examples.fact: Section 253 can allow draft stopping-up work to begin while a planning application is in progress, but the order cannot be made until planning permission has been granted.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 248 distinction
official_measurement_examples.fact: Section 248 addresses highways affected by construction or improvement of another highway and has different statutory tests from section 247.

official_measurement_examples.name: Public-interest assessment
official_measurement_examples.fact: Transport order decision-making considers impacts on highway users and public interest rather than re-determining the merits of the underlying planning permission.

official_measurement_examples.name: Conditional implementation
official_measurement_examples.fact: A made stopping-up order can contain implementation conditions; the existence of an order is not always proof that highway rights have already ceased.

official_measurement_examples.name: Planning-highway separation
official_measurement_examples.fact: Planning permission and highway stopping-up rights are separate legal controls; one does not silently substitute for the other.

official_measurement_examples.name: Parcel limitation
official_measurement_examples.fact: A stopping-up order does not establish freehold ownership, access over private land, infrastructure delivery or final development yield.

core_rules: planning permission does not remove highway rights
draft order is not made order
made order is not necessarily implemented order
highway rights are distinct from freehold ownership
stopping up does not create private access rights
transport order does not re-determine planning merits
London procedures can differ from outside Greater London
PROW status and stopping-up order status remain distinct
highway closure does not calculate development yield
no parcel highway-rights clearance or Future Growth score may be promoted while recovery is parked
current order status must be case-specific
